entities.name: Giulio Gabrielli the Younger
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Giulio Gabrielli the Younger (1748 – September 26, 1822) was an influential Italian cardinal whose career spanned the tumultuous period of the Napoleonic Wars and the subsequent Restoration of the Papal States. Born into a noble family in Fano, Papal States, Gabrielli rose through the ranks of the Roman Curia, becoming a cardinal-priest in 1801 under Pope Pius VII. His unwavering loyalty to the papacy and his steadfast opposition to French imperial ambitions made him a central figure in the Church's resistance against Napoleon Bonaparte's attempts to subjugate the Holy See, leading to his imprisonment and exile.

Gabrielli's most defining period began in 1808 when, serving briefly as Secretary of State, he became a direct antagonist to Napoleon. He refused to swear allegiance to the French Empire, maintaining the temporal sovereignty of the Pope. This defiance resulted in his arrest in Rome and subsequent imprisonment, first in Milan, then in France, alongside Pope Pius VII himself, and later in Corsica. During this forced exile, he continued to counsel the pontiff and uphold papal authority, symbolizing the Church's spiritual and political resilience against secular encroachment. His steadfastness earned him deep respect within the curia and among Catholic faithful.

Upon the fall of Napoleon and the Congress of Vienna in 1815, Gabrielli returned to Rome, playing a significant role in the re-establishment of the Papal States and the reorganization of the Roman Curia. He served as Prefect of the Congregation of the Council from 1814 until his death, overseeing matters of ecclesiastical discipline and jurisprudence. His experience under duress and his commitment to traditional papal prerogatives influenced the conservative direction of the Church in the early post-Napoleonic era, contributing to the strengthening of papal absolutism and the suppression of liberal movements within the Church.
